June 15, 2026 
 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0062-P 
P.O. Box 8013 
Baltimore, MD 21244-8013 
 
Re: 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed 
Rule [CMS-0062-P] 
 
Dear Administrator: 
 
As members of the Healthy Aging Coalition, we advance policy and knowledge that support 
healthy aging and longevity. Our coalition includes a range of stakeholders, including 
researchers, clinicians, academic leaders, industry experts, advocacy and community-based 
organizations, foundations, businesses, faith-based organizations, and government leaders – all 
committed to the shared vision of promoting healthy lifestyles and aging with dignity and 
independence. 
We write in response to the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for 
Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P), published on April 10, 2026. Prior authorization (PA) 
reform is central to our mission to assure access and credible information to promote choice and 
consumer decision making. The healthcare professionals who serve older adults – including 
primary care providers, nurses, physical and occupational therapists, behavioral health clinicians, 
and social workers – are among those most burdened by PA processes, and it is the consumer 
that is most impacted by delays or denial of necessary care.  
It is with a consumer focus, that we commend CMS for continuing to build on the 2024 final rule 
(CMS-0057-F) and offer the following comments on three specific areas: 
 
I. Assure Data Transparency is Findable and Accessible to Improve Access for Consumers. 
To achieve this goal, CMS Should Require Consistent Public Posting Standards and 
Establish a Centralized Database 
 
CMS-0057-F required impacted payers to publicly report prior authorization metrics on their 
websites by March 31, 2026. Despite this mandate, compliance has been deeply problematic – 
not because payers failed to post data, but because the data is difficult for consumers, 
researchers, advocates, and policymakers to find and use. 
Our experience monitoring payer compliance with CMS-0057-F revealed that payers have 
satisfied the letter of the requirement however data has been buried within dense plan 
documents, posted under inconsistent or obscure headings, nested multiple levels deep within 
carrier websites, and formatted in ways that resist comparison across plans. A beneficiary 
 
 
attempting to evaluate their Medicare Advantage plan’s prior authorization practices – the very 
population CMS intended to protect –faces obstacles in locating this information. 
We find that transparency needs to be enhanced and improved.  CMS-0062-P has an opportunity 
to correct this by establishing meaningful accessibility standards. We recommend that CMS: 
• 
Require consistent labeling and site architecture. CMS should mandate that all impacted 
payers post PA metrics under a standardized, required heading (e.g., “Prior Authorization 
Metrics” or “Prior Authorization Transparency Report”) accessible from a prominent 
location on the plan’s homepage or member portal, reachable within no more than two 
clicks. Standardized file formats (e.g., machine-readable CSV or JSON in addition to 
PDF) should be required to enable independent analysis. 
• 
Establish a CMS-operated centralized public database. CMS should collect all impacted 
payer PA metric submissions and consolidate them into a single, publicly accessible, 
searchable database hosted on CMS.gov. A centralized repository would dramatically 
improve public access, enable plan-to-plan comparisons, support independent research, 
facilitate regulatory oversight, and enhance access for  beneficiaries and advocates 
attempting to track down disparate data sources. This approach mirrors the precedent set 
by CMS for other data transparency initiatives, including the Open Payments database 
and the Medicare Provider Utilization and Payment Data program. 
The requirement in CMS-0062-P for impacted payers to report API endpoint information to 
CMS for publication in a centralized location (proposed under the Payer Reporting of API 
Endpoints section) demonstrates that CMS already recognizes the value of centralization. We 
urge CMS to extend this logic to PA metrics data, where the need for centralized access is 
equally compelling and the public interest is so important. 
 
II. Medicare Part D Drug PA Metrics Should Be Subject to Meaningful Consumer-
Accessible Transparency Requirements 
 
CMS-0062-P proposes to extend PA transparency requirements to drugs covered under the 
medical benefit for impacted payers, while explicitly excluding Medicare Part D drugs covered 
under MA-PD plans on the grounds that they are subject to existing Part D reporting 
requirements and that adding new requirements would be duplicative and burdensome. 
The Healthy Aging Coalition respectfully disagrees with this exclusion and urges CMS to 
reconsider. 
Existing Part D reporting requirements – including aggregated coverage determination, 
redetermination, and reopening data submitted to CMS – do not meet the transparency goals 
advanced by CMS-0062-P. Specifically: 
• 
Part D coverage determination data is not publicly posted in a consumer-accessible 
format. Unlike the website posting requirements finalized in CMS-0057-F and proposed 
in CMS-0062-P, Part D data is submitted to CMS for regulatory purposes but is not made 
available to beneficiaries, caregivers, advocates, or researchers in a meaningful way. 
 
 
• 
Existing Part D data does not include prior authorization metrics – specifically, the 
prior authorization approval rates, denial rates, and overturn rates on appeal that CMS has 
correctly identified as essential to assessing payer performance and identifying potential 
for patient harm. A beneficiary or their physician seeking to understand how aggressively 
a particular MA-PD plan uses PA for their needed medications has no practical means to 
access that information. 
• 
The exclusion creates a significant information gap for older adults. Prescription drugs 
are among the most common healthcare needs for Medicare beneficiaries, and drug PA is 
a frequent source of delay, disruption, and harm. Excluding MA-PD drug PA from public 
transparency requirements leaves beneficiaries less informed about a PA domain that is 
highly consequential for their health and daily lives. 
The argument that new requirements would be “duplicative” is not persuasive where existing 
requirements serve a different and more limited purpose. CMS has the authority – and the 
responsibility – to ensure that PA transparency requirements for drugs are as robust, consumer-
accessible, and analytically useful as those being proposed for non-drug items and services. 
We recommend that CMS: 
• 
Require MA-PD plans to publicly post prior authorization metrics for Part D drugs on 
their websites on the same schedule and in the same format as other impacted payers, 
consistent with the requirements proposed in CMS-0062-P and finalized in CMS-0057-F. 
• 
Include Part D drug PA data in any centralized CMS database established pursuant to 
Section I above, so that beneficiaries can make meaningful comparisons across plans at 
the point of enrollment. 
III. The Healthy Aging Coalition Supports Proposed Requirements for Numeric Count 
Reporting of Prior Authorization Metrics for Non-Drug Items and Services 
The Healthy Aging Coalition supports CMS's proposal to require reporting of numeric counts for 
prior authorization requests, approvals, denials, and appeals. Numeric reporting will provide 
policymakers, beneficiaries, researchers, and other stakeholders with greater visibility into prior 
authorization practices and will facilitate more meaningful oversight of utilization management 
activities. 
However, aggregate numeric counts alone are insufficient. CMS should require reporting entities 
to provide prior authorization data by major service category, including at a minimum: inpatient 
hospital services, outpatient services, pharmacy services, behavioral health services, skilled 
nursing and rehabilitation services, and other post-acute care services. 
Recent reports from the HHS Office of Inspector General (OIG) illustrate why service-level 
transparency is essential. In June 2026, OIG reported that Medicare Advantage organizations 
overturned 95 percent of appealed prior authorization denials for skilled nursing facility (SNF) 
admissions and concluded that "the extremely high overturn rate of appealed SNF admission 
denials raises concerns that more initial SNF requests should have been approved rather than 
denied because the MAO ultimately determined the requested care was medically necessary." 
 
 
The report further noted that these findings raise concerns regarding denials that were never 
appealed. Similar OIG analyses identified concerning denial and overturn patterns for inpatient 
rehabilitation facilities and long-term acute care hospitals. 
These findings demonstrate that aggregate reporting can mask significant problems affecting 
specific categories of care. A health plan may report overall denial and appeal rates that appear 
reasonable when viewed in the aggregate, while simultaneously exhibiting unusually high denial 
rates or overturn rates in particular service categories. Without service-specific reporting, 
regulators, beneficiaries, providers, and researchers would be unable to identify these patterns or 
assess whether certain populations or types of care are disproportionately affected by prior 
authorization practices. 
Accordingly, CMS should require that all publicly reported prior authorization metrics be 
segmented by service category. Such reporting would align with OIG's recommendations that 
CMS collect and analyze prior authorization data by standardized service type and would 
provide the transparency necessary to identify concerning utilization management practices and 
ensure timely access to medically necessary care. 
Summary 
 
The Healthy Aging Coalition appreciates the opportunity to comment on CMS-0062-P. We are 
committed to a prior authorization system that is transparent, efficient, and centered on the needs 
of older adults. The recommendations outlined above—requiring standardized and centralized 
public access to prior authorization data, extending meaningful transparency requirements to Part 
D drugs, and finalizing numeric count reporting requirements that include reporting by service 
category—are practical, achievable steps that will strengthen accountability, improve oversight, 
and help ensure timely access to medically necessary care. By adopting these recommendations, 
CMS can provide beneficiaries, caregivers, providers, researchers, and policymakers with a more 
complete and meaningful understanding of how prior authorization policies affect access to care 
across the Medicare program. 
If you require additional information, please contact the Healthy Aging Coalition’s CEO, Vicki 
Shepard, at vicki.shepard@comcast.net. 
 
Respectfully, 
 
HEALTHY AGING COALITION MEMBERS AND FRIENDS

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Healthy Aging Coalition Members and Friends, led by Vicki Shepard, Founder and CEO, Healthy Aging Coalition.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group; coalition including researchers, clinicians, academic leaders, industry experts, community-based organizations, foundations, businesses, faith-based organizations, and government leaders.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Coalition members include leaders from aging, clinical, community health, research, philanthropy, and advocacy organizations focused on healthy aging and longevity.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The Healthy Aging Coalition supports CMS's prior authorization reform goals but urges CMS to make transparency data findable, centralized, standardized, and useful to older adults and advocates. The Coalition asks CMS to extend consumer-accessible PA metrics to Medicare Part D drugs and require PA metric reporting by service category rather than only aggregate counts.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING by analogy to centralized publication; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; TRANSPARENCY; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL to the extent the proposal covers medical benefit drugs; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations are discussed in detail; references CMS-0062-P, CMS-0057-F, MA-PD, and Medicare Part D reporting.
- **Standards referenced:** Machine-readable CSV or JSON formats; public posting standards; CMS.gov centralized database. No FHIR IG or NCPDP standard is materially addressed.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Centralized and Findable Public PA Metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Existing PA metrics posted under CMS-0057-F are often buried, inconsistently labeled, hard to compare, and inaccessible to beneficiaries and researchers.
- **Specific request:** Require standardized headings and site architecture, prominent links within no more than two clicks, machine-readable CSV/JSON in addition to PDFs, and a CMS-operated searchable public database.

**Topic 2: Extend Transparency to Part D Drug PA Metrics**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify/Oppose exclusion
- **Rationale:** Existing Part D coverage determination data is not public in a consumer-accessible format and does not provide PA approval, denial, and overturn metrics.
- **Specific request:** Require MA-PD plans to publicly post Part D drug PA metrics on the same schedule and format as other impacted payers and include that data in any centralized CMS database.

**Topic 3: Numeric Count Reporting for PA Metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Numeric counts improve oversight, but aggregate counts can mask service-specific access problems.
- **Specific request:** Finalize numeric counts for PA requests, approvals, denials, and appeals, and segment all publicly reported PA metrics by major service category.

**Topic 4: Service-Level Transparency**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** High denial or overturn rates may be hidden in aggregate reporting even when specific care categories, such as SNF admissions, show concerning patterns.
- **Specific request:** Require reporting by inpatient hospital, outpatient, pharmacy, behavioral health, skilled nursing/rehabilitation, post-acute, and other major service categories.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S24:** Recommends specific public posting content and format for PA transparency data, including standardized labels and machine-readable CSV/JSON.
- **S26:** Supports standardized file formats and site architecture to enable comparison and independent analysis.
- **S27:** Implies consistent schedule alignment across payer types, including MA-PD Part D drug PA metrics.
- **S29:** Supports numeric counts and recommends major service category segmentation.
- **S34:** Supports regular public reporting in a standardized location and centralized CMS database.
- **S35:** Supports CMS publication of aggregated and payer-specific data through a searchable public repository.
- **S28/S31 by implication:** Opposes excluding MA-PD Part D drugs from transparency requirements and argues existing Part D reporting is not duplicative.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Require standardized PA metric labels and website architecture.
2. Require payer PA metrics to be available within no more than two clicks from a prominent plan webpage or member portal location.
3. Require machine-readable CSV or JSON in addition to PDF.
4. Establish a CMS-operated, centralized, searchable database for PA metrics.
5. Require MA-PD plans to publicly report Part D drug PA metrics.
6. Include Part D drug PA data in the centralized CMS database.
7. Finalize numeric count reporting for PA requests, approvals, denials, and appeals.
8. Require PA metrics to be segmented by major service category.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Transparency data is technically posted but difficult to find or use; Part D exclusion creates a major information gap; aggregate data masks service-specific problems.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Older adults and caregivers cannot compare plans or understand PA practices; medically necessary care may be delayed or denied without meaningful accountability.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Inconsistent payer website architecture, obscure headings, inaccessible formats, and fragmented data sources.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** June 2026 OIG report found MA organizations overturned 95 percent of appealed SNF admission PA denials.
- **Studies or research referenced:** HHS OIG reports on SNF admissions, inpatient rehabilitation facilities, and long-term acute care hospitals.
- **Examples provided:** PA metrics buried in dense plan documents; data nested deep on carrier websites; Part D data submitted to CMS but not meaningfully available to beneficiaries.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Medicare beneficiaries, older adults, caregivers, healthcare providers, researchers, advocates, policymakers, MA-PD plans, and impacted payers.
- **Economic implications:** Centralized transparency may increase compliance work for payers but improve oversight, plan comparison, and accountability.
- **Technical feasibility:** Practical and achievable; the commenter points to CMS's proposed centralized API endpoint reporting as a model.
- **Patient care impact:** Strongly positive if CMS makes PA practices visible by plan, drug/service type, and service category.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, consumer-focused, policy-oriented.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "The data is difficult for consumers, researchers, advocates, and policymakers to find and use." - Context: Critiquing current PA metric posting.
2. "The Healthy Aging Coalition respectfully disagrees with this exclusion and urges CMS to reconsider." - Context: Opposing exclusion of Medicare Part D drug PA metrics.
3. "Aggregate numeric counts alone are insufficient." - Context: Arguing for service-category reporting.
4. "A centralized repository would dramatically improve public access" - Context: Supporting a CMS-operated public database.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Focuses on older adults' access to medications and medically necessary care.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Core theme: findable, accessible, centralized, comparable PA metrics.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Consumer focus includes beneficiaries and older adults who may be less able to navigate obscure data.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Notes clinicians serving older adults are burdened by PA and need usable transparency.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Recommends machine-readable formats and a centralized CMS database.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for CMS collection and publication of payer data for public use.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Highlights gap created by excluding Part D drug PA metrics while adding medical benefit drug transparency.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Addresses current public posting workflows and Part D reporting limitations.
